synopsis: Across construction, mining and on-road studies, synthetic data is supported as training augmentation rather than a replacement for real data: studies from 2023–2026 report benefits from mixing, but persistent gaps with synthetic-only training and benefits that depend on detector family [f6685, f6686, f6689, f7047, f7057]. Reported examples include 50% fewer real images and a 16% detector improvement in a 2023 construction study, cited through a 2025 secondary summary, and a 2025 study whose best result used 1,500 real plus 1,500 synthetic images [f7049, f7050, f7051]. Visual realism does not establish detector validity: real-trained radar detectors failed on most simulated vehicles despite improved image similarity, while mining evidence shows degradation in dust in a dataset of 30,000 lidar frames, over 80% dusty [f4423, f4826, f12610]. The recommended training loop anchors simulation in real off-road logs, tests on untouched real data and collects targeted real data for residual gaps; shared training/testing generators or assets can contaminate validation, and new mounting heights require retraining or adaptation rather than threshold changes alone [f7102, f7097, f7037]. Formal or static verification cannot prove recognition of arbitrary real scenes, the cited FDA guidance does not cover a neural-network detector, and manufacturers must address machine-learning vision gaps in test standards with evidence [f668, f7645, f2911]. Retraining can invalidate prior validation, and whether a trained-then-frozen detector is “self-evolving” under EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 remains disputed; the booklet notes deterministic safety channels as a way to avoid placing the entire proof burden on learned perception [f2940, f6700, f12877].
